paragraphs.context: Dear Readers, Hour of the Olympics was a
paragraphs.simple: Mary Pope Osborne says she loved writing this book because Jack and Annie meet her favourite animal from Greek myths. She has written many books that tell Greek myths again. She hopes this book will make you interested in Greek myths. The stories are over 3,000 years old, but they are still full of life and exciting. Reading them is like listening to old Greek storytellers across hundreds of years. That is real time travel!

background.note: The old stories of ancient Greece about gods, heroes and monsters, like Zeus, Hercules and Pegasus.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a
paragraphs.mainIdea: A magic tree house appears in Frog Creek.
paragraphs.simple: One summer day a strange tree house suddenly appeared in the woods of Frog Creek, a town in Pennsylvania.

background.note: Frog Creek is the made-up town where Jack and Annie live. Pennsylvania is a real state in the east of the USA.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, they discovered that the tree
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie learned that the tree house is Morgan le Fay's. She is a magic librarian from the time of King Arthur. She travels through time and space and collects books.

background.note: A magic woman from old British stories about King Arthur. In this series she is a kind librarian.

paragraphs.context: In the Magic Tree House Books #8–12, Jack
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie became Master Librarians.
paragraphs.simple: In earlier books Jack and Annie answered four old riddles, so they became Master Librarians. Morgan gave them secret library cards with the letters M L.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie’s first four missions are to
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie's first four jobs are to save stories from old libraries. This is the fourth one.

paragraphs.context: He threw back his covers and jumped out
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushed back the blankets on his bed and jumped up. He was already wearing his jeans and T-shirt.

paragraphs.context: “I didn’t want to waste any time,” said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack did not want to lose time.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said he did not want to lose any time. He put on his backpack.

paragraphs.context: “Sure. Put it in your backpack,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said yes, and gave Jack her card to put in his backpack. She would carry the flashlight.

paragraphs.context: “All set,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: "Ready," said Jack.

paragraphs.context: They tiptoed downstairs and out the door.
paragraphs.simple: They walked on their toes down the stairs and out of the door, so nobody would hear.

paragraphs.context: They followed the beam of light across their
paragraphs.simple: They followed the line of light from the flashlight across the yard and up the street.

paragraphs.context: Jack was thrilled to be going to ancient
paragraphs.simple: Jack was very happy and excited to go to ancient Greece. But he was worried about one thing.

paragraphs.context: “What do you think will happen after we
paragraphs.simple: Jack asked Annie what would happen after Greece. Was this their very last mission?

paragraphs.context: They started running. The flashlight beam flew in
paragraphs.simple: They began to run. The light of the flashlight moved in front of them and showed them the way.

paragraphs.context: They slowed to a walk when they got
paragraphs.simple: They walked slowly when they got to the Frog Creek woods. The woods were completely black.

paragraphs.context: “You’re very brave to say that,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said they were very brave to say that. They have had three very hard trips as Master Librarians.

paragraphs.context: “You risked your life to save the lost
paragraphs.mainIdea: They saved the story of Hercules.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said they put their lives in danger to save the lost story of Hercules.

background.note: A very strong hero in Greek and Roman myths. Jack and Annie saved his story in Pompeii in book 13.

paragraphs.context: “It was nothing,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: "It was easy; you don't need to thank us," said Annie.
paragraphs.tone: "It was nothing" is a polite, modest answer when someone thanks you.

paragraphs.context: “And the Chinese story of the silk weaver,”
paragraphs.simple: Morgan thanked them for the Chinese story of the silk weaver and the Irish story of the sea snake Sarph.

background.note: A girl in a Chinese love story (the Weaver Girl, Zhinü, and the Cowherd). Jack and Annie saved it in book 14.
A sea serpent in an old Irish story. Jack and Annie saved it in book 15.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard a rustling sound.
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard a soft sound, like paper moving.

paragraphs.context: Jack took the book from her. Annie shined
paragraphs.simple: Jack took the book. Annie put the light on the cover. The title was A Day in Ancient Greece.

paragraphs.context: “But in our darkest hour, only the lost
paragraphs.mainIdea: Only the lost story can help in the worst time.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said: but in our worst, most hopeless time, only the lost story can save us.

paragraphs.context: Jack shivered with excitement as he pointed at
paragraphs.simple: Jack shook a little because he was so excited. He pointed at the cover of the book.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was silent.
paragraphs.simple: Then there was no sound at all.
paragraphs.tone: Every trip ends like this. Here the book says "silent" (no sound) instead of "still" (not moving).

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. Warm sunshine streamed into
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his eyes. Warm sunlight came into the tree house.

paragraphs.context: “We sure don’t need the flashlight here,” he
paragraphs.mainIdea: They do not need the flashlight.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they really did not need the flashlight here.

paragraphs.context: His clothes were similar to the ones he’d
paragraphs.simple: Jack's clothes were like the clothes he wore in the Roman town of Pompeii: a long loose shirt and open shoes. Instead of his backpack he had a leather bag again.

background.note: A Roman town in Italy. A volcano covered it with ash in the year 79. Jack and Annie went there in book 13.

paragraphs.context: “And we landed in an olive tree—just like
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is in an olive tree.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said they had landed in an olive tree, just like in Pompeii.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out the window. He caught his
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked out. He stopped breathing for a moment because he was so surprised.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t know,” said Annie. “Look past the
paragraphs.simple: Annie said to look past the trees. It looked like a big outdoor event with games and food.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked. Annie was right. Past the olive
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see tents, buildings and crowds.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was right. Past the olive trees there was a field full of white tents. Behind the field were red brick buildings with tall stone posts and lots of people.

paragraphs.context: The Olympic Games began in ancient Greece over
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Olympic Games began in Greece.
paragraphs.simple: The book said: The Olympic Games began in ancient Greece more than 2,500 years ago. Every four years, more than 40,000 people went to Olympia, the town where the sports festival happened.

background.note: A place in the south-west of Greece with temples and sports grounds. The Olympic Games were held there. The modern Olympics are named after it.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man,” Jack whispered. “We’re at the ancient
paragraphs.simple: Jack said very quietly, "Wow! We are at the ancient Olympics!"

paragraphs.context: Jack heard pipe music and smelled food roasting
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard music played on pipes and smelled food cooking over fires. Groups of men talked to each other in an excited way.

paragraphs.context: “That’s funny,” said Annie. “I don’t see any
paragraphs.simple: Annie said it was strange: she did not see any girls.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around. But he only saw men
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked around. He only saw men and boys. There were no women or girls at all.

paragraphs.context: Then he saw an outdoor theater. A woman
paragraphs.simple: Then Jack saw a theater outside, with no roof. A woman was standing on the stage. She had yellow hair and a purple tunic.

background.note: Greek theaters were outside, with stone seats in a half circle on a hill.

paragraphs.context: A soldier was on the stage with her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A soldier is on the stage.
paragraphs.simple: A soldier was on the stage with her. He wore a long cape. His face was hidden by a helmet with red feathers or hair on top.

paragraphs.context: “I think they’re doing a play,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought they were acting a play. He said he would look in the book.

paragraphs.context: The Greeks were the first to write plays.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Greeks wrote the first plays.
paragraphs.simple: The book said: The Greeks were the first people to write plays. Many English words about the theater come from Greek words, like drama, scenery and chorus. People still act many Greek plays today.

paragraphs.context: When Jack looked up, he saw the woman
paragraphs.mainIdea: The woman is really a boy.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack looked up, the woman had pulled off her false hair. It was a boy wearing a woman's clothes!

paragraphs.context: “See, even she’s a boy,” said Annie. “That’s
paragraphs.simple: Annie said, "See? Even she is a boy. That is very strange."

paragraphs.context: A few actors would play many different parts
paragraphs.simple: The book said: A few actors played many different people in one play. Women could not act, so men also played the women in the play.

background.term: Women were not allowed to act
background.note: In ancient Greece only men could act. They wore masks and costumes to play women.

paragraphs.context: “That’s not fair,” said Annie. “What if a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks it is not fair.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said it was not fair. What if a woman wanted to act in a play?
paragraphs.tone: This is the main idea of the book: girls in ancient Greece could not do many things. Annie is angry about it.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry about it,” said Jack. He put
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to see the Olympics.
paragraphs.simple: Jack told Annie not to worry. He put the book away. He said they should have a quick look at the Olympics and then find their story.

paragraphs.context: He nudged Annie to move along.
paragraphs.simple: Jack gave Annie a small push with his arm, so she would walk on.

paragraphs.context: They turned around. A man with a short
paragraphs.mainIdea: A man with a beard comes.
paragraphs.simple: They turned around. A man with a short white beard was walking to them.

paragraphs.context: “Who are you?” Annie asked boldly.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asked bravely, "Who are you?"
paragraphs.tone: Annie is not afraid. She asks the man the same question he asked her.

paragraphs.context: “My name is Plato,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: The man said his name was Plato.

background.note: A famous Greek thinker who lived about 2,400 years ago (427–347 BC). He started a school in Athens called the Academy.

paragraphs.context: “You may have heard of me,” the man
paragraphs.simple: The man said, "Maybe you have heard of me. I am a philosopher."

paragraphs.context: “A lover of wisdom,” said Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said a philosopher is someone who loves wisdom.

background.note: The word "philosopher" comes from Greek: "philo" = love and "sophia" = wisdom.

paragraphs.context: “It’s odd to see a girl walking so
paragraphs.mainIdea: Plato is surprised to see a girl.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said it is strange to see a girl walking so bravely in Olympia. She must come from far away.

paragraphs.context: “I think we should show him our cards,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: They should show Plato their cards.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said quietly that they should show him their cards, because he is a lover of wisdom.
paragraphs.tone: Morgan told them to show the cards to the wisest person they meet. Annie thinks a philosopher must be wise.

paragraphs.context: The letters M and L that stood for
paragraphs.simple: The letters M and L, for Master Librarian, shone on the cards.

paragraphs.context: “Amazing!” said Plato. “I’ve never met such young
paragraphs.simple: Plato said, "Wonderful! I have never met such young Master Librarians. Why are you in Olympia?"

paragraphs.context: “Oh, yes,” said Plato softly. “This was written
paragraphs.simple: Plato said softly that the story was written by a very clever poet, who is really his friend.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, but I must warn you—never tell anyone
paragraphs.simple: Plato said he will take them, but they must never tell anyone who the poet is. It is a secret.

paragraphs.context: They started down a dirt road. It was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many people are going to the games.
paragraphs.simple: They walked down a road of earth. It was full of people going to the games.

paragraphs.context: He opened the door and led Jack and
paragraphs.simple: Plato opened the door and took Jack and Annie into an empty open space in the middle of the house.

paragraphs.context: Rooms opened onto the sunny courtyard. Everything was
paragraphs.simple: The rooms opened onto the sunny courtyard. Everything was quiet.

paragraphs.context: Men and women lived in separate parts of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Greek girls could not go to school.
paragraphs.simple: The book said: men and women lived in different parts of a Greek house. Women spent most of their time making thread, making cloth and looking after the kitchen. Boys went away to school at seven. Girls could not go to school.

paragraphs.context: “Girls can’t go to school?” said Annie. “How
paragraphs.simple: Annie asked, "Girls can't go to school? Then how do they learn to read and write?"

paragraphs.context: At that moment Plato returned. With him was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Plato comes back with a woman.
paragraphs.simple: Just then Plato came back. A young woman was with him. She wore a long tunic with a coloured edge, and she was holding a scroll.

paragraphs.context: “Jack and Annie, meet our secret poet,” said
paragraphs.mainIdea: The secret poet is a woman.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said, "Jack and Annie, this is our secret poet."
paragraphs.tone: Surprise! The secret poet is a young woman. That is why she must be a secret.

paragraphs.context: “She wrote a poem and brought it to
paragraphs.mainIdea: The poet brought her poem to Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said she wrote a poem and brought it to him, because he has written and said that Greek girls should go to school and learn things.

background.term: Greek girls should go to school
background.note: The real Plato wrote, in his book "The Republic", that women could do the same jobs as men if they were taught.

paragraphs.context: “It’s a wonderful story,” said Plato. “But she
paragraphs.mainIdea: The poem must go far away.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said it is a wonderful story. But she will have problems if people in Greece read it. They must take it to their faraway home, where it will be safe.

paragraphs.context: “I cannot,” she said. When she saw Annie’s
paragraphs.simple: The woman said she could not. When she saw Annie's sad face, she said they could tell people it was written by Anonymous.

paragraphs.context: “No, anonymous means that no one knows who
paragraphs.simple: Plato said "anonymous" means nobody knows who wrote it.

paragraphs.context: “I’m afraid the risk is too great,” said
paragraphs.simple: Plato said he was sorry, but the danger is too big.

paragraphs.context: The poet smiled at her. “I am happy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Women will write books one day.
paragraphs.simple: The poet smiled. She was happy that her story would go to their country. She said maybe one day women everywhere will write books, like men.

paragraphs.context: “They will,” said Jack. “I promise.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack said, "They will. I promise."
paragraphs.tone: Jack knows the future: today women write many books. The poet cannot understand this.

paragraphs.context: “Thank you, Annie,” the young woman said. “And
paragraphs.simple: The young woman thanked Annie and Jack. She bent forward politely and hurried out of the courtyard.

paragraphs.context: “Girls can’t write stories,” grumbled Annie. “They can’t
paragraphs.simple: Annie said in a low, unhappy voice: girls can't write stories, can't go to school, can't be in plays. She was tired of ancient Greece and wanted to leave.

paragraphs.context: “Well,” said Plato slowly. “I would like to
paragraphs.simple: Plato said slowly that he would like to take them both to the games. He has special seats in a place for important people. But... and he looked at Annie.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t tell me,” she said. “Girls can’t go
paragraphs.mainIdea: Girls can't go to the games.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said, "Don't tell me. Girls can't go to the Olympics either."

paragraphs.context: “A girl will get in terrible trouble if she goes
paragraphs.simple: Plato said a girl will have terrible problems if she goes to the games.

background.term: A girl will get in terrible trouble
background.note: In ancient Olympia, married women could not watch the games. There were separate games for girls, called the Heraia.

paragraphs.context: Annie sighed. “It’s really, really not fair,” she
paragraphs.simple: Annie let out a long, sad breath and said it was really, really not fair.

paragraphs.context: “I’m sorry,” said Plato. “My country is a
paragraphs.simple: Plato said he was sorry. His country is a democracy, and they believe in freedom for their citizens. But right now only men are citizens.

background.note: The word comes from Greek: "demos" = people, "kratos" = power. Athens had the first democracy about 2,500 years ago.

paragraphs.context: “No, Jack. You go to the Olympics,” said
paragraphs.simple: Annie said Jack should go to the Olympics. He could at least tell her about it. He should write notes.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t want to leave Annie alone. But
paragraphs.simple: Jack did not want to leave Annie alone. But he also did not want to miss the Olympics.

paragraphs.context: He and Jack turned and joined the crowd
paragraphs.simple: Plato and Jack turned and walked with the crowd that was going to the Olympic sports area.

paragraphs.context: “This is the very first day of the
paragraphs.simple: Plato told Jack this was the very first day of the games, the day of the chariot races.

background.note: Races with small two-wheeled carts pulled by four horses. They were the most exciting and dangerous event at Olympia.

paragraphs.context: He couldn’t believe he was going to see
paragraphs.mainIdea: There are no chariot races today.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not believe he would see a chariot race. The modern Olympic Games do not have chariot races.

paragraphs.context: “That is the gymnasium,” he said. “It is
paragraphs.simple: Plato said: that is the gymnasium, where our athletes practise. They practise running and throwing the javelin and discus.

background.note: A Greek word. In ancient Greece it was a place for sport and also for learning.

paragraphs.context: “People all over the world copy us Greeks,”
paragraphs.simple: Plato said people all over the world copy the Greeks.
paragraphs.tone: Plato is proud, and it is true: the gym, the Olympics, and many words come from Greece.

paragraphs.context: “Okay, we can go,” said Jack. He tucked
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they could go now. He put his notebook under his arm.

paragraphs.context: “The olive tree is our sacred tree,” he
paragraphs.simple: Plato said the olive tree is a holy tree for them. The winners of the games will wear crowns made from its branches.

background.note: The winners at ancient Olympia did not get gold medals. They got a crown of olive leaves.

paragraphs.context: Next they passed a beautiful statue of a
paragraphs.mainIdea: A statue of a lady with wings.
paragraphs.simple: Next they walked past a beautiful statue of a lady with wings.

paragraphs.context: “She’s Nike, the goddess of victory,” said Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said she is Nike, the goddess of winning.

background.note: The Greek goddess of victory. Say it /ˈnaɪki/. The sports company Nike took its name from her.

paragraphs.context: He took Jack to a brick building with
paragraphs.simple: Plato took Jack to a brick building with huge columns. It was a temple. Jack breathed in fast in surprise.

paragraphs.context: In front of them loomed the biggest statue
paragraphs.simple: In front of them stood the biggest statue Jack had ever seen, tall and a little scary.

paragraphs.context: The statue was at least two stories high.
paragraphs.simple: The statue was at least as high as a two-floor building. It was a man with a beard sitting on a king's chair.

paragraphs.context: “This is the temple of Zeus. And that
paragraphs.simple: Plato said this is the temple of Zeus, and that is a statue of Zeus. The Olympic Games are held to honour him. He is the most important of all the Greek gods and goddesses.

background.note: The king of the Greek gods, the god of the sky and thunder. His huge gold and ivory statue at Olympia was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

paragraphs.context: “Yesterday all the athletes came here,” said Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said that yesterday all the athletes came here. They promised Zeus that they had practised for ten months, and that they would follow the rules of the games.

paragraphs.context: The statue of the mighty Greek god stared
paragraphs.mainIdea: The statue looks down at Jack.
paragraphs.simple: The statue of the great, strong Greek god looked down at Jack.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, trumpet sounds came from outside.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly they heard trumpets outside.

paragraphs.context: “The hour has come,” said Plato. “We must
paragraphs.simple: Plato said the time had come. They must hurry, because the Olympic parade was starting.

paragraphs.context: Plato and Jack hurried past the crowds standing
paragraphs.simple: Plato and Jack hurried past the people standing at the sides of the race track. Everyone was shouting and cheering.

paragraphs.context: “I have seats next to the judges,” said
paragraphs.simple: Plato said he has seats next to the judges. He pointed to a tall building with rows of long seats.

paragraphs.context: He had a great view.
paragraphs.simple: He could see very well from there.

paragraphs.context: The Olympic parade had already started. Musicians playing
paragraphs.simple: The Olympic parade had already started. Musicians playing pipes walked in front. Behind them walked the Olympic athletes, the best in all of Greece.

paragraphs.context: “The athletes in front are the runners,” said
paragraphs.simple: Plato said the athletes in front are the runners. Running races are the oldest event of the Olympics.

background.note: The first Olympic Games in 776 BC had only one event: a running race of about 192 metres, called the "stade". The word "stadium" comes from it.

paragraphs.context: “Behind the runners are the boxers,” said Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said the boxers come behind the runners. They wear special gloves and helmets of bronze.

paragraphs.context: “Behind them are the wrestlers,” said Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said the wrestlers come behind them.

paragraphs.context: When Jack looked up again, he saw a
paragraphs.simple: When Jack looked up again, he saw a soldier at the side of the track looking up at him.

paragraphs.context: The soldier was dressed like the actor from
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soldier looks like the actor.
paragraphs.simple: The soldier was dressed like the actor from the outdoor theater. He had a long cape and a helmet with a red top that hid most of his face.

paragraphs.context: “Here come the discus and javelin throwers,” said
paragraphs.simple: Plato said the discus and javelin throwers come next, and then the men in armor.

paragraphs.context: “They race wearing full armor,” said Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said they race wearing all their metal armor.

background.note: The "hoplite race" was a real Olympic race. Runners wore a helmet and carried a heavy shield.

paragraphs.context: “In a moment, the chariot races will begin,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Winning a chariot race is the greatest honor.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said the chariot races will begin soon. Winning a chariot race is the biggest honour of the games.

paragraphs.context: Jack just nodded. He was still studying the
paragraphs.simple: Jack only nodded. He was still looking carefully at the short soldier, who seemed to look back at him.

paragraphs.context: Jack gasped. It was Annie’s hand waving!
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed in fast in surprise. It was Annie's hand waving!

paragraphs.context: Jack stared in horror at Annie. She must
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked at Annie in great fear. She must have taken a costume from the theater!

paragraphs.context: He remembered Plato’s words: A girl will get
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembered what Plato said: a girl will be in terrible trouble if she tries to go to the Olympic Games.

paragraphs.context: Jack shook his head at her and pointed
paragraphs.simple: Jack shook his head at her and pointed, as if he was saying, "Get out of here!"

paragraphs.context: Jack kept shaking his head at Annie. He
paragraphs.simple: Jack kept shaking his head at Annie. He even shook his closed hand at her.

paragraphs.context: “Of course not,” said Plato. “We take the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Greeks take the games seriously.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said, "Of course not. We think the games are very important."
paragraphs.tone: Funny misunderstanding: Jack is shouting at Annie, but Plato thinks Jack is talking to him about the games.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt his face grow hot. He glared
paragraphs.simple: Jack felt his face become hot. He looked at Annie's back angrily.

paragraphs.context: “The chariots are taking their places,” said Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said the chariots were going to their starting places.

paragraphs.context: Jack saw the dozens of chariots lined up
paragraphs.simple: Jack saw lots of chariots in a line on the race track. Four horses pulled each chariot.

paragraphs.context: Jack glanced back at Annie. She was looking
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked quickly back at Annie. She was looking up at him and pointing at the chariots.

paragraphs.context: The horses took off!
paragraphs.simple: The horses started running very fast!

paragraphs.context: The crowd went wild. They were cheering and
paragraphs.simple: The crowd became very excited and noisy. They cheered, screamed and hit the ground hard with their feet.

paragraphs.context: Clouds of dust rose up as the chariots
paragraphs.simple: Clouds of dust went up as the chariots raced around the track.

paragraphs.context: A few people began staring at the strange
paragraphs.simple: Some people began looking at the strange little soldier with the high voice.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t take it anymore. He had to
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not stand it any longer. He had to get Annie away before it was too late!

paragraphs.context: He shoved his notebook into his bag.
paragraphs.simple: He pushed his notebook into his bag quickly.

paragraphs.context: Jack was afraid to tell him that Annie
paragraphs.simple: Jack was afraid to tell Plato that Annie had done something against the rules.

paragraphs.context: “Have a safe journey,” said Plato.
paragraphs.simple: Plato said, "Have a safe trip."

paragraphs.context: Her pigtails flew up and down as she
paragraphs.simple: Her hair, tied in two pigtails, flew up and down as she jumped and shouted, "Go! Go! Go!"

paragraphs.context: Now lots of people were staring at her.
paragraphs.simple: Now many people were looking at her. Someone shouted for the guards.

paragraphs.context: Annie was too busy cheering to notice anything.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was so busy cheering that she did not see anything.

paragraphs.context: But two big guards got to Annie first.
paragraphs.simple: But two big guards got to Annie before Jack.

paragraphs.context: “Let go of me!” she shouted.
paragraphs.simple: "Stop holding me!" she shouted.

paragraphs.context: Jack rushed down the steps of the viewing
paragraphs.simple: Jack ran down the steps of the seats.

paragraphs.context: “Leave her alone!” Jack yelled.
paragraphs.simple: "Don't touch her! Go away from her!" Jack shouted.

paragraphs.context: His voice was lost in the noise of
paragraphs.simple: The race was so noisy that no one heard his voice.

paragraphs.context: He pushed his way through the crowd.
paragraphs.simple: He pushed people to move through the crowd.

paragraphs.context: Finally, Jack reached Annie and the guards. He
paragraphs.simple: At last Jack got to Annie and the guards. He tried to take her, but a guard stood in his way.

paragraphs.context: More guards arrived. The crowd began to shout
paragraphs.simple: More guards came. The crowd started to shout, "Take her away! Take her away!"

paragraphs.context: Of course! thought Jack. The poet’s story! This
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought, "Of course! The poet's story! This is surely our worst time!"

paragraphs.context: But Jack’s voice was again lost in the
paragraphs.simple: But again no one heard Jack, because the race was so loud. The chariots with four horses raced fast through the dust.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around wildly for someone—or something—to help
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked all around in a worried way for someone, or something, to help them.

paragraphs.context: Then suddenly the crowd fell silent.
paragraphs.simple: Then suddenly the crowd became quiet.

paragraphs.context: All heads turned to watch as a huge
paragraphs.simple: Everyone turned to look as a huge white horse ran very fast out of the dust.

paragraphs.context: The crowd murmured with excitement and wonder.
paragraphs.simple: The crowd talked softly. They were excited and full of wonder.

paragraphs.context: The guards stared in awe at the horse.
paragraphs.simple: The guards looked at the horse in wonder and fear.

paragraphs.context: Annie broke free and dashed over to Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pulled herself away from the guards and ran fast to Jack. He took her hand and they ran to the horse.

paragraphs.context: The horse reared and pawed the air.
paragraphs.simple: The horse stood up on its back legs and hit the air with its front feet.

paragraphs.context: The guards froze.
paragraphs.simple: The guards stopped and did not move.

paragraphs.context: Then the white horse leaped forward, pulling the
paragraphs.simple: Then the white horse jumped forward, pulling the chariot behind him.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t even wave back at Plato. All
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not even wave to Plato. He could only hold on very tightly as the horse ran fast next to the Olympic racers.

paragraphs.context: Jack bounced up and down. Dust and sand
paragraphs.simple: Jack moved up and down. Dust and sand got in his eyes. He closed his eyes tightly and made himself low in the chariot.

paragraphs.context: He didn’t know where they were going. But
paragraphs.simple: Jack did not know where they were going, but it was not important. The white horse was the one who decided.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard the thundering noise of the racing
paragraphs.simple: Jack heard the very loud noise of the racing horses and chariots. He heard the crowd screaming.

paragraphs.context: He felt sand blowing in his face and
paragraphs.simple: He felt sand blowing in his face, and the chariot hitting the ground and shaking noisily.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, he was thrown backward. He heard a
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly he was thrown back. He heard a rushing sound of wind, then...

paragraphs.context: The white horse had grown giant feathery wings
paragraphs.simple: The white horse now had giant wings with feathers, and it was pulling their chariot into the sky.
paragraphs.tone: This is the big surprise: the horse is Pegasus, the flying horse from Greek myths.

paragraphs.context: Jack gripped the railing of the chariot and
paragraphs.simple: Jack held the bar on the side of the chariot very tightly, as if his life depended on it.

paragraphs.context: Below, the Olympic crowd watched in stunned silence.
paragraphs.simple: Below them, the Olympic crowd watched without a word, too surprised to speak.

paragraphs.context: The winged horse left the games behind and
paragraphs.simple: The horse with wings left the games and flew over the temple of Zeus, the statue of Nike, the holy olive tree and the gymnasium.

paragraphs.context: Finally, the winged horse coasted to the ground
paragraphs.simple: At last the horse with wings came down smoothly to the ground near the olive trees.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie stepped out of the chariot.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie stepped out of the chariot. Jack's legs were shaking so much that he almost could not walk.

paragraphs.context: Annie rushed to the horse and stroked his
paragraphs.simple: Annie ran to the horse and moved her hand gently along his neck.

paragraphs.context: The horse snorted and pawed the ground.
paragraphs.simple: The horse made a loud sound through its nose and hit the ground with its foot.

paragraphs.context: Her eyes filled with tears.
paragraphs.simple: Tears came into Annie's eyes.

paragraphs.context: The horse put his head down and touched
paragraphs.simple: The horse put his head down and touched Annie's forehead with his soft nose. Then he gave her a kind little push toward the tree house.

paragraphs.context: Annie sniffled but started walking. Jack took her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie walks to the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Annie breathed in through her nose because she was crying, but she started walking. Jack held her hand.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out the window. The horse had
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked out of the window. The horse had opened his big wings and was rising from the field.

paragraphs.context: The white horse flew high into the blue
paragraphs.mainIdea: The horse flies into the sky.
paragraphs.simple: The white horse flew high into the blue sky over Olympia.

background.note: "Olympian" means of Olympia, or of Mount Olympus, the home of the Greek gods.

paragraphs.context: A tear rolled down her cheek.
paragraphs.simple: A tear ran down Annie's face.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was still.
paragraphs.simple: Then nothing moved at all.

paragraphs.context: “I did one fun thing,” Annie said wistfully.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said a little sadly that she did one fun thing: she rode in a chariot pulled by a flying horse.

paragraphs.context: “That must have been wonderful,” said Morgan. “You
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said that must have been wonderful. They were very lucky to bring her the story of Pegasus.

background.note: The white flying horse of Greek myths. Say it /ˈpegəsəs/.

paragraphs.context: “I know,” said Morgan. “Many talented women used
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many women used the name Anonymous.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said she knew. In the past, many women with great skill used that name. Her story will be a great new book for Morgan's library in Camelot.

background.note: King Arthur's castle in old British stories. Morgan's library is there.

paragraphs.context: “Ah, my good friend Plato,” said Morgan. “He
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said Plato was her good friend. He was one of the greatest thinkers who ever lived.

paragraphs.context: “You can,” Morgan said softly. “He’s here right
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said softly that Annie can see him. He is here now.

paragraphs.context: Annie switched off the light.
paragraphs.simple: Annie turned off the flashlight.

paragraphs.context: “In the night, you can see all the
paragraphs.mainIdea: All the story characters are here.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said that at night they can see all the story people and animals who saved them on their four missions: Hercules, the silk weaver, Sarph the sea serpent, and Pegasus.

paragraphs.context: Has Morgan gone crazy? wondered Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wondered if Morgan had gone mad.

paragraphs.context: “Look up,” said Morgan. “Your friends are in
paragraphs.simple: Morgan told them to look up. Their friends are in the night sky. They are stars.

paragraphs.context: He stared at the shimmering field of tiny
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked at the many tiny stars shining softly above him.

paragraphs.context: “Hercules is a constellation,” said Morgan. “The Romans
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said Hercules is a group of stars. The Romans saw him in the sky, down on one knee, holding a big stick over his head.

background.note: There really is a group of stars called Hercules in the northern sky.

paragraphs.context: “And there’s the silk weaver, with her beloved
paragraphs.mainIdea: The silk weaver and the cowherd.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said there is the silk weaver with the cowherd she loves. The old Chinese said they were two stars, one on each side of the Milky Way.

background.term: the silk weaver, with her beloved cowherd
background.note: In Chinese they are Zhinü and Niulang (the stars Vega and Altair). They meet once a year on the Qixi Festival.
The long band of light across the night sky. It is made of billions of stars.

paragraphs.context: “And long ago, the Irish believed the Milky
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said the Irish long ago believed the Milky Way was the sea serpent Sarph.

paragraphs.context: She waved her hand again and the white
paragraphs.simple: Morgan waved her hand again, and the white horse's head, wings and running legs shone in the sky.

paragraphs.context: Jack thought he saw the stars move as
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought he saw the stars move, as if Pegasus was standing up on his back legs in the sky.

paragraphs.context: After a breathless moment of silence, Morgan lowered
paragraphs.simple: After a moment so exciting that no one breathed, Morgan put her arm down. The night sky was just a field of tiny shining stars again.

paragraphs.context: “You have done amazing work as Master Librarians,”
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said they had done wonderful work as Master Librarians. She would give them any important mission.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled with relief.
paragraphs.simple: Jack smiled. He was no longer worried.

paragraphs.context: “As soon as I need your help, I
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said that as soon as she needs their help, she will ask them to come. Now they should go home and rest.

paragraphs.context: “Farewell,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: "Goodbye," said Morgan.

paragraphs.context: There was a sudden rushing of wind, then
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly there was fast wind and a very bright light they could not see through. Then Morgan and the magic tree house were gone.

paragraphs.context: The night was still.
paragraphs.simple: The night was quiet, and nothing moved.

paragraphs.context: But he didn’t ask Annie to turn on
paragraphs.simple: But Jack did not ask Annie to turn on the flashlight. This time, for once, he was not worried about finding the way home.

paragraphs.context: Morgan’s words came back to him: The old
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembered Morgan's words: the old stories are always with us. We are never alone.
paragraphs.tone: This is the message of the book: old stories stay with us and help us.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up at the stars again. They
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked up at the stars again. They were becoming weaker as the morning light got stronger.

paragraphs.context: But he thought he could hear the beating
paragraphs.simple: But he thought he could hear big wings moving up and down, somewhere high above.

paragraphs.context: The Olympics of ancient Greece were held for
paragraphs.simple: The Olympics of ancient Greece happened for more than a thousand years, from 776 BC to AD 394.

background.note: "B.C." means before the birth of Jesus Christ; "A.D." means after it. So the games lasted about 1,170 years.

paragraphs.context: For two months, all fighting and wars ceased
paragraphs.simple: For two months all fighting and wars stopped, so people could travel safely to and from the Olympics.

background.note: This was called the "Olympic Truce". Cities at war agreed to stop fighting.

paragraphs.context: The first modern Olympics were held in Athens
paragraphs.simple: The first modern Olympics were in Athens, Greece, in 1896.

background.note: The capital city of Greece, then and now.

paragraphs.context: Greek athletes believed that having a physically fit
paragraphs.simple: Greek athletes believed a healthy, strong body was a way to show respect to their main god, Zeus. The statue of Zeus at Olympia was one of the seven wonders of the old world. Sadly, it is gone now.

background.term: the seven wonders of the ancient world
background.note: A list of seven amazing buildings and statues of the ancient world. Only the Great Pyramid of Egypt is still standing.

paragraphs.context: The word anonymous comes from a Greek word
paragraphs.simple: The word "anonymous" comes from a Greek word that means "with no name".

paragraphs.context: The word museum is also of Greek origin.
paragraphs.simple: The word "museum" also comes from Greek. More than 2,000 years ago the Greeks built a temple to nine goddesses called the Muses. They called the temple the Museum.

background.note: Nine Greek goddesses of art, music, poetry and learning.

paragraphs.context: Some Greek letters are similar to ours. The
paragraphs.simple: Some Greek letters look like ours. The Greek A is alpha and the B is beta. That is where the word "alphabet" comes from.

paragraphs.context: About 2,500 years ago, the Greeks adopted a
paragraphs.simple: About 2,500 years ago the Greeks started a way of ruling called democracy. All citizens could help decide what the government did. But women and slaves were not citizens.

paragraphs.context: Plato the philosopher lived in ancient Greece in
paragraphs.simple: Plato lived in Greece in the 300s BC. He started a school called the Academy. In his teaching and writing he thought about the best way to run a government. People still talk about his ideas today.

paragraphs.context: Zeus was god of the skies and ruler
paragraphs.simple: Zeus was god of the sky and ruler of all the Greek gods. They were called Olympians because they lived on Mount Olympus. Later the Romans took the main Greek gods as their own. The Romans called Zeus "Jupiter".

background.note: The highest mountain in Greece. In myths the gods lived on top of it.

paragraphs.context: In Greek mythology, a great winged horse sprang
paragraphs.simple: In Greek myths, a great horse with wings jumped out of the neck of Medusa, a monster with snakes for hair. The horse was called Pegasus, maybe from a Greek word for "spring" (water coming out of the ground). A young man called Bellerophon made Pegasus gentle and rode him.

background.note: A monster in Greek myths with snakes for hair. Anyone who looked at her turned to stone.

paragraphs.context: In ancient times, mythic characters from different world
paragraphs.simple: Long ago, people in many cultures saw characters from their myths as groups of stars in the night sky. When a hero or heroine got a place in the sky, he or she was famous forever.

sentences.simple: These stories are more than 3,000 years old, but they are still some of the most lively and exciting stories we have.
sentences.main: They are still some of the most exciting tales.

parts.meaning: But sadly, today only men get this freedom.

parts.text: as the horse galloped beside the Olympic racers.

darkest hour.meaning: The worst and most hopeless time, when you think nothing can help you any more.

darkest hour.usageNote: A strong, a little old-fashioned phrase. In this series it is the time when the magic story can help.

light the way.meaning: To give light so that people can see where to go.
light the way.example: The flashlight beam flew in front of them, lighting the way.
light the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

pull on.meaning: To put on clothes or a bag quickly.
pull on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

throw back.example: He threw back his covers and jumped out of bed.
throw back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

it was nothing.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

take place.example: the town where the festival of athletic games took place
take place.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

dress up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take a peek.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

take care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get in trouble.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at least.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

line up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

let go of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

leave her alone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

push his way through.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.
